assessment.name: AT2: Blues to Jazz
assessment.due: Part A Week 7, Part B Weeks 9 to 10

lessons.title: AT2 issued, both parts at once
lessons.contentPoint: Reflecting on and documenting process
lessons.intention: We are learning what AT2 asks for and how its two parts fit together.
criteria: I can explain what Part A and Part B each require and when each is due.
steps: Assessment Task 2 issued, both parts published together so students know from the first lesson that the piece they write is the piece they will play.
The blueprint handed over with the notification: the progression, the piano voicings, the drum pattern and the walking bass rules.
The process log restarted for this task, with checkpoints set for Weeks 3, 6 and 8.
lessons.enduring: Documenting the process is part of composing, not a report on it afterwards.

lessons.title: The 12-bar blues, heard and counted
lessons.contentPoint: How genre and style are characterised
lessons.intention: We are learning to hear and count the 12-bar blues form.
criteria: I can count a 12-bar chorus and say where chords IV and V arrive.
steps: The 12-bar form heard in three recordings from the register, counted aloud, then diagrammed on the board.
How the genre is characterised: what makes a listener say this is a blues within two bars.
Students count a full chorus without the teacher and mark where the chord changes fall.
resources: Listening set from the repertoire register.
lessons.enduring: A genre is recognisable because of features that can be named.

body.lead: We are learning to hear and count the 12-bar blues form.

clauses.text: The 12-bar form heard in three recordings from the listening set, counted aloud together, then diagrammed on the board bar by bar.
How the genre is characterised: what makes a listener say “this is a blues” within two bars. Name the features rather than the feeling.
Count a full chorus without the teacher, and mark where the changes to chord IV and chord V fall.

criteria: I can count a 12-bar chorus without help.
I can say where chords IV and V arrive.

lessons.title: Playing the 12-bar form
lessons.contentPoint: Conventions of a period, genre or style
lessons.intention: We are learning to play the 12-bar blues with the conventions of the style.
criteria: I can play my part through a full chorus with a swing feel.
steps: The whole room plays the 12-bar form: chords, bass, drums and a riff, with parts matched to ability.
The conventions of the style applied as they are played: swing feel, backbeat, dynamics that build across a chorus.
Repeated until the room can start and finish together without counting aloud.
lessons.enduring: Playing a style means applying its conventions, not only its notes.

lessons.title: Roman numerals I, IV and V
lessons.contentPoint: How genre and style are characterised
lessons.intention: We are learning to name chords by their function in the key.
criteria: I can label a progression with Roman numerals and transpose it.
steps: Roman numerals attached to chords the class already plays, then to the blues form.
Why numerals rather than letters: the form transposed to two more keys in the same lesson.
Written work: label the chords in three supplied progressions.
lessons.enduring: Naming a chord by its function is what lets a form move between keys.

lessons.title: The blues scale in the hands
lessons.contentPoint: Conventions of a period, genre or style
lessons.intention: We are learning to play the blues scale and hear its blue notes.
criteria: I can play the blues scale in one key and find the blue notes in it.
steps: The blues scale learned by playing it in one key across the room's instruments, then heard in the repertoire.
Blue notes located and bent or leaned on, so the sound is experienced before it is defined.
Call and response using only the scale, teacher to class.
lessons.enduring: The scale is a sound before it is a set of notes.

lessons.title: Aural routine: swing, syncopation and backbeat
lessons.contentPoint: How genre and style are characterised
lessons.intention: We are learning to hear and name the rhythmic features of this style.
criteria: I can tell a swung excerpt from a straight one and say what makes it swing.
steps: Aural routine continues from Term 1 with this term's content: straight against swung quavers, identified by ear.
Syncopation and backbeat named in short excerpts and clapped back.
Written into the flat.io aural notebook.
lessons.enduring: The features that define a style can be heard, named and reproduced.

lessons.title: Riffs and bass lines transcribed by ear
lessons.contentPoint: Transcribing using relevant notations
lessons.intention: We are learning to write down what we hear using the right notation.
criteria: I can transcribe a two-bar riff accurately enough for someone to play it.
steps: Short riffs and bass lines transcribed by ear straight into flat.io, in the notation the style actually uses.
Transcription method taught: find the first note, find the shape, then fix the rhythm.
Checkpoint 1 of the process log.
lessons.enduring: Transcription is listening made permanent.

lessons.title: The blues' West African roots
lessons.contentPoint: Music influencing and challenging ideas
lessons.intention: We are learning where the blues came from and what it carried with it.
criteria: I can describe two features of the blues and trace each to its source.
steps: Where this music came from: call and response, blue notes and the relationship between work song, spiritual and the blues.
West African musical practice studied in its own right, from the repertoire register, not only as a source.
This carries the global music culture repertoire area for Year 9.
resources: Listening set from the repertoire register.
lessons.enduring: Music carries the history of the people who made it.

lessons.title: Music that carried a people's story
lessons.contentPoint: Music influencing and challenging ideas
lessons.intention: We are learning how music can influence and challenge ideas.
criteria: I can explain how a piece of music affected the people who heard it.
steps: How this music influenced and challenged ideas well beyond where it started, at local, national and international levels.
One recorded example examined for what it was for, who it was for, and what changed because of it.
Written response: two well-formed dot points on context.
lessons.enduring: Music does work in the world, not only in the room.

lessons.title: Improvising over the form: first choruses
lessons.contentPoint: Improvising to develop ideas
lessons.intention: We are learning to improvise inside a form.
criteria: I can play one chorus of improvisation that stays in the scale and leaves space.
steps: Everyone improvises. One chorus each over the backing, using the blues scale and nothing else.
The rule taught first: play fewer notes and leave space, because the form is doing half the work.
Recorded, so students hear their own first attempt.
lessons.enduring: Improvising is composing at speed inside rules everyone knows.

lessons.title: Head, solos, head
lessons.contentPoint: Manipulating elements when improvising and performing
lessons.intention: We are learning to manipulate the elements while improvising.
criteria: I can change one element deliberately during my solo and name it afterwards.
steps: The structure of a jazz performance: head, solos, head, and who signals each change.
The class plays the whole structure with three soloists, then swaps.
Elements manipulated deliberately in the solo: dynamics and register chosen in advance.
lessons.enduring: A solo is shaped, not simply filled.

lessons.title: Walking bass: root on the change
lessons.contentPoint: Manipulating elements when improvising and performing
lessons.intention: We are learning how a walking bass line is built.
criteria: I can build a walking bass line that lands on the root at every change.
steps: The walking bass rules supplied and applied: root on the change, approach the next chord by step or semitone.
Everyone plays a walking bass line on their own instrument, at pitch or in octaves.
The rules written into the process log for use in Part A.
resources: Bass, keys and low register instruments.
lessons.enduring: A simple rule, applied consistently, produces a line that works.

lessons.title: Comping, and the voicings supplied
lessons.contentPoint: Manipulating elements when improvising and performing
lessons.intention: We are learning to accompany a soloist rather than to play under them.
criteria: I can comp behind a soloist without covering them.
steps: The supplied piano and guitar voicings taught and played, with the rhythmic placement that makes them comping rather than strumming.
Comping behind a soloist: listening for space and staying out of the melody's register.
Elements manipulated while accompanying: dynamics, texture and density.
lessons.enduring: Accompaniment is a set of decisions made in real time.

lessons.title: Trading fours
lessons.contentPoint: Improvising to develop ideas
lessons.intention: We are learning to improvise responsively rather than in turn.
criteria: I can answer another player's four bars with something related to them.
steps: Four-bar phrases traded between players, then between a player and the drums.
Listening as the condition of the exercise: the answer has to respond to the question.
Recorded and played back, with two dot points on what was answered.
lessons.enduring: Improvisation is a conversation when the players are listening.

lessons.title: Jazz drum notation
lessons.contentPoint: Transcribing using relevant notations
lessons.intention: We are learning to read and write drum notation on a staff.
criteria: I can read the supplied jazz drum pattern and notate it correctly.
steps: Jazz drum notation formalised out of Year 8's beat grids: the ride pattern, the backbeat, the hi-hat on two and four.
The supplied drum pattern read from notation and played, then written out from memory.
Notation entered into flat.io using the drum staff.
lessons.enduring: A grid and a staff say the same thing, and the staff travels further.

lessons.title: Taking a risk in a solo
lessons.contentPoint: Creative risk and audience response
lessons.intention: We are learning to take creative risks and strengthen musical intent.
criteria: I can take a deliberate risk in a solo and carry it through.
steps: Creative risk in improvisation: what happens when a player leaves the scale, and how they get back.
Each student takes one deliberate risk in a chorus, and the class names what it did to the audience.
Discussion: a wrong note held with confidence and a wrong note flinched at are different events.
lessons.enduring: Risk taken deliberately is part of performing, not a failure of accuracy.

lessons.title: Recreating two supplied melodies
lessons.contentPoint: Manipulating elements to create musical ideas
lessons.intention: We are learning how a blues head is built before we write one.
criteria: I can reproduce a supplied head accurately and describe how it is made.
steps: Two supplied blues heads recreated note for note in flat.io, before any original writing.
What each head does with the elements: range, rhythm, repetition and where it leaves space for the response.
Students annotate both with what they intend to borrow.
resources: flat.io files of the two heads.
lessons.enduring: Copying a model accurately is how the model becomes usable.

lessons.title: The class band plays a standard
lessons.contentPoint: Creative risk and audience response
lessons.intention: We are learning to perform a complete piece with intent.
criteria: I can play a full performance with the band and say what we set out to communicate.
steps: The class band plays one jazz standard from the register end to end, with solos.
Performance intent named before playing: what should this audience feel by bar 24?
Checkpoint 2 of the process log.
lessons.enduring: A performance is aimed at somebody.

lessons.title: Composing the 16-bar blues: melody first
lessons.contentPoint: Sound sources and digital technologies
lessons.intention: We are learning to compose a melody over a given harmonic frame.
criteria: I can write a 16-bar melody that fits the progression and has a shape.
steps: Part A composition begins. Melody written first over the supplied progression, in flat.io.
Elements manipulated deliberately: register, rhythm, repetition and where the phrase ends.
Sound sources and playback used to test rather than to decorate.
resources: flat.io template with the progression already entered.
lessons.enduring: Composing inside a frame that already works is where the musical decisions become visible.

lessons.title: Writing the bass and the drum part
lessons.contentPoint: Writing for the performers' capabilities
lessons.intention: We are learning to write parts that the people in this room can play.
criteria: I can write a bass and drum part that my classmates can read and play.
steps: Walking bass written using the supplied rules; drum part entered from the supplied pattern and varied.
Writing for the capability of the actual player: range, hand position, and what is possible at tempo.
Students consult the classmate who will play each part.
lessons.enduring: A composer writes for the performer, not for the page.

lessons.title: AT2 Part A due
lessons.contentPoint: Reflecting on and documenting process
lessons.intention: We are learning to submit composed work with the record of how it was made.
criteria: I can submit a complete score and a log that shows my decisions.
steps: Part A submitted: the 16-bar blues in flat.io with melody, walking bass and drum part, plus the process log.
Log read alongside the score, so the decisions and the artefact are marked together.
Students state one thing they expect to have to change.
lessons.enduring: The log is assessed evidence, not a rough draft of the piece.

lessons.title: Part A feedback: is it playable
lessons.contentPoint: Writing for the performers' capabilities
lessons.intention: We are learning to judge our own writing against what a player can do.
criteria: I can identify what in my piece is unplayable and say how I will fix it.
steps: Marked Part A returned this week, a fortnight before Part B, so an unplayable piece can still be fixed.
Feedback focused on playability: range, tempo, page turns, and whether the drum part is humanly possible.
Each student logs the feedback and the plan.
lessons.enduring: Marking Part A before Part B is played is what makes the fix possible.

lessons.title: Fixing the unplayable
lessons.contentPoint: Working safely and respectfully with others
lessons.intention: We are learning to work on each other's music respectfully and usefully.
criteria: I can give and take feedback on a piece without taking over it.
steps: Revision workshop. Players and composers work in pairs, and the player reads the part aloud on their instrument.
Protocols for working on somebody else's work: what may be suggested and what is the composer's call.
Revised files saved as a new version so the change is visible in the log.
lessons.enduring: Working respectfully with others is a condition of workshopping music.

lessons.title: Rehearsing your own blues
lessons.contentPoint: Performing in a range of styles, including own compositions
lessons.intention: We are learning to perform our own compositions with an ensemble.
criteria: I can rehearse my own piece with the band and direct the tempo and feel.
steps: The class band rehearses the student compositions, two or three per lesson from here on.
Performing your own composition: the composer counts it in and takes responsibility for the tempo.
Checkpoint 3 of the process log.
lessons.enduring: Hearing your own writing played is the fastest feedback there is.

lessons.title: AT2 Part B performances, day 1
lessons.contentPoint: Performing in a range of styles, including own compositions
lessons.intention: We are learning to perform our own composition in a range of styles.
criteria: I can perform my own piece with the band, including an improvised chorus.
steps: Part B begins: each student's own blues performed with the class band, including one improvised chorus.
Assessed against the criteria issued in Week 1.
Audience protocol maintained, and every performance recorded.
lessons.enduring: The piece a student wrote and the piece a student plays should be the same piece.

lessons.title: AT2 Part B performances, day 2
lessons.contentPoint: Performing in a range of styles, including own compositions
lessons.intention: We are learning to present and perform our own work to an audience.
criteria: I can introduce my piece and perform it under assessment conditions.
steps: Performances continue.
Each composer introduces their piece in one sentence: what it is for and what to listen for.
Marking notes taken live against the criteria.
lessons.enduring: Presenting the work is part of performing it.

lessons.title: Listening back to your own performance
lessons.contentPoint: Evaluating own performances and compositions
lessons.intention: We are learning to evaluate our own performances and compositions from a recording.
criteria: I can separate what my piece does from how I played it.
steps: Each student listens to their own recording and writes two dot points on it, one on the composition and one on the performance.
Reflection distinguishing the two: a good piece played badly and a weak piece played well sound different.
Entries filed in the process log.
lessons.enduring: You hear your own work differently once it is a recording.

lessons.title: AT2 Part B performances, day 3
lessons.contentPoint: Performing in a range of styles, including own compositions
lessons.intention: We are learning to perform our own compositions to a finished standard.
criteria: I can perform my piece as a finished item rather than as a draft.
steps: Final performances, including any deferred or rescheduled.
The class band plays two of the strongest student pieces again for the room.
Recording archived for the process log and for the Year 10 handover.
lessons.enduring: A piece is finished when it has been played well, not when it has been written.

lessons.title: Evaluating the elements in our blues
lessons.contentPoint: Analysing elements in own and others' compositions
lessons.intention: We are learning to analyse the elements of music in our own and each other's compositions.
criteria: I can discuss how the elements were used in a classmate's piece and in my own.
steps: Three student pieces analysed by the class for how the elements were used, with the composer present and answering.
The same analysis applied by each student to their own piece in writing.
Vocabulary from the term used precisely, and corrected where it is not.
lessons.enduring: Analysing your own work is the same skill as analysing anyone else's.

lessons.title: Feedback used: what would change next time
lessons.contentPoint: Evaluating success and using feedback
lessons.intention: We are learning to use feedback to refine and improve our work.
criteria: I can show what I changed because of feedback and what I would change next.
steps: Final log entry for AT2: what the feedback said, what was changed because of it, and what would change in the next piece.
Success in communicating intent evaluated against what the student said they were aiming at in Week 1.
Term closed by naming what Term 3 needs: the writing, and the aural routine that makes the paper survivable.
lessons.enduring: Feedback that does not produce a change has not been used.
